paragraphs: An agent acting with incomplete observations faces several competing needs: earn rewards, work out its current situation, and learn how its environment behaves. This paper brings these needs into a single Bayesian reinforcement learning model. It extends reasoning about uncertain environments to partially observable settings, where the underlying state is hidden.

The proposed Bayes-Adaptive POMDP lets interactions improve the agent’s model while supporting planning that accounts for the value of those improvements. An action can therefore matter both for its immediate consequences and for what it reveals. The mathematical framework supports optimal action sequences that balance learning the model, identifying the state, and collecting reward.

The authors show how to construct a finite approximation while preserving the value function, and describe approximations for belief tracking and planning. In experiments on two domains, both model estimates and returns improve as learning proceeds. These findings illustrate the framework’s intended connection between better knowledge and better decisions, while the practical algorithms use approximations to the underlying model.
neurips-2007-bayes-adaptive-pomdps-25928.tldr: Bayes-Adaptive POMDPs combine learning an uncertain environment with planning under hidden states, balancing information gathering and reward.

paragraphs: Hierarchical clustering describes data through nested groups, represented as a tree. This paper gives that tree a Bayesian treatment by using Kingman’s coalescent as a prior. The prior provides a probabilistic starting point for possible hierarchies, so the clustering problem becomes inference about a tree rather than simply a sequence of grouping decisions.

The authors develop two inference approaches that construct the hierarchy from the bottom upward by merging groups. One is greedy, committing to choices as construction proceeds. The other uses sequential Monte Carlo, a sampling approach to inference. Both retain the agglomerative structure of repeatedly combining smaller groups into larger ones within the proposed probabilistic model.

The paper reports experimental superiority over the state of the art and demonstrates applications to document clustering and phylolinguistics. These examples show the model being used to organize both documents and language relationships. The central contribution is the combination of a tree prior with workable bottom-up inference methods; the reported performance advantage is an experimental finding.
neurips-2007-bayesian-agglomerative-clus.tldr: A Bayesian hierarchy model based on Kingman’s coalescent supports bottom-up clustering algorithms with reported experimental advantages.

paragraphs: Models of neural responses often have many possible stimulus features but relatively few experimental observations. This paper gives generalized linear models of spiking neurons a Bayesian treatment that addresses both feature selection and uncertainty. Instead of reporting only fitted weights, the method approximates the posterior distribution over all weights using expectation propagation.

A Laplacian prior favors sparse solutions, helping exclude features that do not critically influence neural activity. This makes the resulting model easier to interpret and supports prediction. The posterior also supplies uncertainty intervals, allowing the authors to assess the statistical significance of estimated effects rather than treating every fitted relationship as equally well supported.

The authors apply the method to recordings from multiple retinal ganglion cells and use parameter uncertainty to evaluate functional couplings between neurons. They also use sparsity to select informative filters from a spike-triggered covariance analysis. Together, these applications show how selecting a smaller set of features and quantifying uncertainty can support neural analysis when observations are limited relative to model size.
neurips-2007-bayesian-inference-for-spik.tldr: Bayesian spiking-neuron models combine sparse feature selection with uncertainty estimates to interpret stimulus responses and functional couplings.

paragraphs: Stochastic planning can be expressed as parameter estimation in an artificial statistical model. This perspective makes inference algorithms available for learning policies, or rules for choosing actions. The paper builds on that connection by observing that the control problem can be viewed as inference across spaces of different dimensions.

That interpretation leads to a reversible jump Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithm, which can move between dimensions during sampling. The authors present it as more efficient than the expectation-maximization approaches previously emphasized for this formulation. It also supports fully Bayesian policy search using a single Markov chain and does not require gradients.

A key feature is sampling directly from a distribution proportional to reward. This focuses inference on outcomes according to their reward contribution, which matters when rewarding events are rare. The paper reports better performance than classic simulation methods in that situation. The contribution is therefore both a reinterpretation of control as trans-dimensional inference and an algorithm whose sampling distribution addresses rare rewards.
neurips-2007-bayesian-policy-learning-wi.tldr: Reversible jump MCMC enables gradient-free Bayesian policy search and improves on classic simulation methods when rewards are rare events.

paragraphs: A linear-nonlinear model describes neural firing as a nonlinear function of a few relevant stimulus components. The practical challenge is identifying those components from neural recordings. This paper compares objectives for doing so with natural stimuli, placing least-squares fitting and information maximization within the same family of Rényi-divergence objectives.

The authors show that the order-two objective is equivalent to least-squares fitting. They then derive errors in the recovered stimulus dimensions in the limit of large spike counts. Within this analysis, order one, corresponding to Kullback–Leibler divergence and mutual-information maximization, produces the smallest reconstruction errors. The theoretical preference is thus tied to a specific asymptotic comparison.

Numerical experiments with model visual neurons examine low signal-to-noise conditions, including few spikes and increasing neural noise. Both least squares and information maximization perform well with small spike counts, but information maximization gives a slight, statistically significant improvement. These results indicate that, for this task, an information-based objective need not require more data than least squares to work effectively.
neurips-2007-better-than-least-squares-c.tldr: Information maximization yields the smallest asymptotic reconstruction errors in the studied objective family and slightly outperforms least squares in neural simulations.

paragraphs: This paper treats classification as a compression decision. For each candidate class, it asks how many extra bits would be needed to encode a new sample while allowing a specified amount of distortion. The sample is assigned to the class with the smallest increase in coding length, yielding the Minimum Incremental Coding Length criterion.

The authors prove asymptotic optimality for Gaussian data and analyze connections to established classifiers, including maximum a posteriori classification and regularized discriminant analysis. They also relate the criterion to clustering through lossy compression. The theoretical guarantee is specific to Gaussian data in the asymptotic setting, while the broader connections explain how familiar classification ideas fit a compression perspective.

Allowing lossy encoding creates a regularization effect that stabilizes the implicit density estimate when samples are scarce. Compression also supplies a common way to handle classes with different dimensions. The basic criterion and its kernel and local variants perform competitively on synthetic data and images of handwritten digits and faces, without using domain-specific information.
neurips-2007-classification-via-minimum-.tldr: MICL classifies a sample by the smallest additional lossy coding cost, connecting compression with regularized classification.

paragraphs: The paper studies the computational difficulty of deciding whether agents can obtain positive expected reward in a partially observable stochastic game. Partial observability means decisions must be made without complete access to the underlying situation. The question concerns the existence of a suitable strategy, rather than the measured performance of a particular learning algorithm.

For the cooperative version, also called a DEC-POMDP, this decision problem was already known to be complete for NEXP. That classification characterizes its worst-case computational difficulty. The unresolved issue addressed here is how the classification changes when cooperation within a group is accompanied by competition between teams.

The authors show that deciding whether one team has a positive-expected-reward strategy in a competitive POSG is complete for NEXP with an NP oracle. An oracle represents access to answers for another class of computational problems. The result identifies the complexity class for the competitive setting and clarifies the role of competition in this already demanding planning problem. It is a complexity-theoretic finding, not an empirical runtime comparison.
neurips-2007-competition-adds-complexity.tldr: Positive-reward strategy existence in competitive partially observable stochastic games is complete for NEXP with an NP oracle.

paragraphs: Mixture-model clustering commonly fits a probabilistic explanation of data using expectation-maximization. Its solution can depend strongly on the initial guess because optimization can settle at a local optimum. This paper addresses that sensitivity by changing the likelihood formulation used for approximate mixture fitting, rather than relying on a different starting point.

The proposed likelihood uses exemplars to approximate the exact mixture likelihood. This produces a convex minimization problem and an efficient algorithm guaranteed to reach its global optimum. The scope of that guarantee matters: it applies to the proposed approximate formulation, rather than establishing global optimization of the original exact mixture likelihood.

The resulting clustering can be interpreted as a probabilistic assignment of data points to exemplars. The objective balances average distance against an information-theoretic cost of that assignment. This gives a concrete interpretation of what the convex problem optimizes. Experiments illustrate the algorithm’s performance and compare it with conventional mixture-model clustering, supporting an assessment of the alternative formulation in practice.
neurips-2007-convex-clustering-with-exem.tldr: An exemplar-based approximation turns mixture fitting into convex clustering with guaranteed convergence to the approximation’s global optimum.

paragraphs: Latent Dirichlet Allocation learns hidden topic structure from text. This paper studies how to fit that model when data are spread across processors, each seeing only part of the collection. The challenge is to make distributed learning behave well despite inference being carried out with locally available data.

The authors propose two approaches. The simpler method runs Gibbs sampling locally and periodically exchanges updates, approximating the behavior of single-processor Gibbs sampling. The second changes the model through a hierarchical Bayesian extension that explicitly accounts for distributed data. It has a theoretical convergence guarantee, but requires a more complex implementation than the approximate method.

Across five real text corpora, distributed learning produces perplexity and precision-recall results indistinguishable from those of single-processor learning. The experiments include computation on 1,000 virtual processors and speedup experiments using 16 processors on a 100-million-word corpus. These findings support distributed LDA as a practical approach in the tested settings, with two distinct choices concerning simplicity, model formulation, and convergence guarantees.
neurips-2007-distributed-inference-for-l.tldr: Two distributed LDA inference schemes preserve single-processor predictive quality in experiments while offering different implementation and convergence trade-offs.

paragraphs: Conditional dependence concerns whether variables remain related after accounting for conditioning information. This paper proposes a measure of that relationship using kernel methods. Its construction uses normalized cross-covariance operators in reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces, providing a way to express statistical relationships through the feature representations associated with kernels.

The central theoretical property is independence from the particular kernel choice in the infinite-data limit, for a wide class of kernels. This distinguishes the proposed measure from earlier kernel dependence criteria. Both qualifications matter: the result concerns the limiting quantity, and the kernels must belong to the class covered by the theory.

The measure also has a straightforward empirical estimate with good convergence behavior, connecting its theoretical definition to calculations from observed samples. The paper discusses its mathematical properties and demonstrates applications experimentally. Its contribution is therefore a conditional-dependence criterion with a stable limiting interpretation across many kernel choices, together with an estimator intended to make that criterion usable with data.
neurips-2007-kernel-measures-of-conditio.tldr: A kernel-based conditional-dependence measure has an empirical estimator and, for a wide kernel class, a kernel-independent infinite-data limit.

paragraphs: This paper develops similarity functions for objects represented as attributed point sets. The points are vectors embedded in Euclidean space, so their positions define which points are neighbors. The approach uses this neighborhood structure to compare whole sets while taking account of information associated with their constituent points.

Two new neighborhood kernels capture different aspects of similarity. One evaluates how alike the attributes are, while the other evaluates shape. The shape comparison is motivated by spectral graph matching techniques. These neighborhood comparisons are used to define positive semidefinite kernels on point sets, giving the similarity construction the mathematical property required for use as such kernels.

The authors test the kernels in face recognition, photo album tagging, and annotation of shots in video sequences, reporting encouraging results. The applications illustrate the value of comparing structured collections through both attributes and spatial relationships. The stated finding supports the approach across these three tasks, without establishing that either neighborhood comparison is universally preferable.
neurips-2007-kernels-on-attributed-point.tldr: Neighborhood-based kernels compare attributed point sets through attribute and shape similarity, with encouraging results on three visual tasks.

paragraphs: A classifier may have abundant training data from one domain but little data from the domain where it will be used. The larger source sample offers more evidence, yet may describe the target poorly. This paper analyzes that tension for learning methods that minimize a weighted combination of source and target training errors.

The authors derive uniform convergence bounds for convex combinations of these empirical risks. Such combinations use nonnegative weights that sum to one. The bounds explicitly account for the trade-off between the amount of source data and its mismatch with the target, alongside the smaller but more directly relevant target sample.

The theory also covers multiple source domains with different sample counts. The authors exhibit cases where unequal weighting of source risks can produce much lower target error than standard empirical risk minimization. This establishes that treating all available training evidence uniformly can be substantially worse in some settings. The result provides a theoretical basis for considering both domain relevance and sample size when combining data.
neurips-2007-learning-bounds-for-domain-.tldr: Domain-adaptation bounds explain how to balance abundant source data against scarce target data and show cases where unequal source weighting helps.

paragraphs: Finding a rare category can be difficult before any examples have been labeled. Randomly inspecting data tends to revisit the dominant category, as with legitimate transactions surrounding unusual fraud patterns. This paper targets the discovery of at least one instance from each minority class, rather than assuming those classes already have labeled representatives.

The method chooses points through an unsupervised strategy based on local differences in density. A nearest-neighbor process varies its scale to favor tightly grouped minority categories. Its rationale depends on the majority class being locally smooth: under that assumption, local density differences can help direct sampling toward compact minority groups.

Experiments on synthetic and real datasets report finding each minority class with only a fraction of the actively sampled points needed by random sampling and Pelleg’s Interleave method. The result indicates that local geometry can make rare-category discovery more sample-efficient in the evaluated settings. The method’s stated structural assumption explains when that geometry is expected to provide useful guidance.
neurips-2007-nearest-neighbor-based-acti.tldr: Variable-scale nearest-neighbor sampling finds rare categories efficiently by exploiting compact minority groups within a locally smooth majority.

paragraphs: Point-process models describe how sensory stimuli relate to the timing of neural spikes. Their success in early sensory pathways has been harder to reproduce in deeper brain regions, partly because standard models omit multiple processing stages. This paper addresses that issue by modeling recorded and unrecorded spiking neurons together.

Including unobserved neurons gives the joint encoding model richer dynamics and more nonlinear stimulus-response behavior. It also allows estimation of connectivity patterns involving both observed and hidden neurons. This makes the model more flexible for fitting neural data and creates a possible route to understanding how networks transform sensory input through interconnected processing.

The authors formulate estimation using variational expectation-maximization and the wake-sleep algorithm. They illustrate performance with a simulated network of two coupled neurons. That demonstration provides a concrete example of the proposed modeling and estimation approach. The broader prospect of gaining insight into sensory computation remains a possibility enabled by the framework, rather than a claim of established biological connectivity recovery.
neurips-2007-neural-characterization-in-.tldr: Jointly modeling observed and hidden spiking neurons adds nonlinear dynamics and enables connectivity estimation in partially recorded populations.

paragraphs: Inference in a discrete Markov random field involves finding probabilities consistent with a joint model. The marginal polytope describes the allowable marginal probabilities, but working with it motivates tractable outer approximations. This paper introduces additional constraints that make those approximations tighter, reducing the set of candidate marginals admitted by the relaxation.

The constraints are derived through projections onto the cut polytope. A cutting-plane algorithm supports efficient optimization over them. Combined with a concave upper bound on entropy, this produces a variational inference algorithm. Tightening the feasible approximation yields tighter upper bounds on the log-partition function, a quantity involved in normalizing the model’s probabilities.

The authors also report that marginal estimates become significantly more accurate experimentally when the tighter bounds are used. They demonstrate benefits for finding the most probable joint assignment, known as MAP inference, in protein structure prediction. The paper therefore connects stronger constraints to both a mathematical improvement in upper bounds and observed improvements in inference quality.
neurips-2007-new-outer-bounds-on-the-mar.tldr: Tighter outer bounds on valid marginals improve variational bounds and empirically strengthen marginal and MAP inference.

paragraphs: Survival analysis with censored observations can be viewed as a ranking task: predictions should order outcomes appropriately even when some event times are only partially observed. The concordance index measures ranking quality and is commonly used to assess survival models. Yet proportional-hazards models are usually trained using Cox’s partial likelihood instead.

This paper examines that difference between the training objective and the assessment measure. The authors derive two bounds on the concordance index and optimize those bounds directly. One follows from properties of proportional-hazards models. The resulting methods connect learning more explicitly to the ranking criterion used to judge the fitted model.

Experiments suggest that the two proposed methods perform similarly, with the new approach giving slightly better results than Cox’s method. The authors also explain why maximizing Cox’s partial likelihood approximately maximizes concordance. That connection helps interpret the modest empirical difference: the conventional training objective already has an approximate relationship to the ranking measure, even though it does not optimize it directly.
neurips-2007-on-ranking-in-survival-anal.tldr: Optimizing concordance-index bounds aligns survival-model training with ranking quality and yields slightly better reported results than Cox’s method.

paragraphs: A receptive field summarizes which stimulus features influence a neuron. Traditional estimates align stimuli with individual spikes, treating each spike as a separate message. This paper broadens that view to activity patterns distributed across neurons or time, asking for a concise description of stimulus processing by an entire population.

The method extends reverse correlation using canonical correlation analysis. It identifies stimulus features and neural response patterns that are most reliably coupled. The resulting population receptive fields span the stimulus subspace most informative about the population response, providing a description that need not be triggered by any single spike.

The authors evaluate the approach with neuronal models and multi-electrode recordings from rabbit retinal ganglion cells. They also extend it using kernel canonical correlation analysis to capture nonlinear stimulus-response relationships and make different coding mechanisms testable. Because the framework operates on multidimensional responses, it can also calculate receptive fields from measurements such as dynamic imaging. The contribution is a shared framework for linking stimulus structure to distributed neural activity.
neurips-2007-receptive-fields-without-sp.tldr: Population receptive fields link stimulus features to distributed neural activity through canonical correlation analysis, with a kernel extension for nonlinear relationships.

paragraphs: This paper seeks candidate regulators using gene-expression data alone. Its hierarchical Bayesian model incorporates the idea that only a few genes act as regulators and that each regulates only a handful of other genes. That assumption shapes the search toward a small collection of regulators with sparse sets of targets.

The authors implement this structure with a spike-and-slab prior formed from Gaussian components of different widths. A hierarchical Bernoulli model controls the mixing weights, connecting the sparsity assumptions at different levels. Expectation propagation provides an efficient inference procedure for estimating the model from expression measurements.

Applied to malaria parasite data, the model identifies candidates with several kinds of biological relevance. Among the top ten genes considered, four have significant homology to transcription factors in an amoeba, one is an RNA regulator, and three have unknown function. These findings give the candidate list biological interest while retaining the paper’s distinction between putative regulators and experimentally established regulatory roles. The model is a discovery tool guided by an explicit sparse-regulation assumption.
neurips-2007-regulator-discovery-from-ge.tldr: A hierarchical sparse Bayesian model uses malaria gene-expression data to identify putative regulators, including candidates related to known regulatory proteins.

paragraphs: Robust regression must distinguish the underlying function from unusual or corrupted observations. This paper uses two Gaussian processes: one models the latent function, and the other controls the mixing weights of a two-component noise model. The second process allows the balance between noise components to vary across the input domain.

This restricted mixture construction gives tractable expectation-propagation updates. The authors report faster inference and model selection, with better convergence than the standard mixture approach. The noise-gating process also lets prior knowledge about the noise domain influence predictions and supplies information about the outlier distribution alongside the predictive distribution.

The model has the same asymptotic computational complexity as conventional robust methods. On benchmarks, it produces more confident predictions than classical heavy-tailed models and improves stability with clustered corruptions, where those models fail in the reported comparison. It also handles smoothly varying noise levels without modification. These findings highlight the benefit of modeling where corruption occurs, while the suggested extensions to more general noise models remain proposals.
neurips-2007-robust-regression-with-twin.tldr: A second Gaussian process models varying noise-mixture weights, improving robust regression stability when corruptions cluster.

paragraphs: High-dimensional prediction can involve more candidate variables than observed examples. This paper introduces sparse additive models, or SpAM, for regression and classification in that setting. The model class combines the variable-selection idea of sparse linear modeling with the flexible response shapes available in additive nonparametric regression.

The additive structure expresses a prediction through contributions from individual covariates, while sparsity limits which contributions are retained. Nonparametric components allow those contributions to take more flexible forms than a single linear coefficient. The combination therefore addresses two aspects of modeling at once: deciding which variables matter and describing how their individual effects vary.

The authors derive a fitting method that remains effective when the number of covariates exceeds the sample size. They also provide a statistical analysis and experiments on synthetic and real data. Those results show that SpAM can effectively fit sparse nonparametric models in high dimensions. The claim concerns this sparse additive approach, whose structure supplies flexibility without requiring every candidate variable to contribute.
neurips-2007-spam-sparse-additive-models.tldr: SpAM combines sparse variable selection with flexible additive effects for prediction even when covariates outnumber samples.

paragraphs: Temporal-difference learning updates value estimates using other estimates as part of its target. Standard TD with eligibility traces includes a learning-rate parameter that controls the size of updates. This paper derives a related update from statistical principles, starting with a variational principle and then applying bootstrapping to discounted state values.

The resulting rule resembles TD(lambda), but replaces the freely chosen learning-rate parameter with an equation specific to each state transition. Updates therefore still have a learning rate; its value is determined by the derived rule. This is the concrete meaning of learning without a learning-rate parameter in the proposed method.

Experiments compare the rule with TD(lambda) and report superior performance in various settings. The authors also make preliminary extensions to reinforcement learning by combining it with Watkins’ Q(lambda) and Sarsa(lambda), again reporting improved performance without a free learning-rate parameter. These findings support the usefulness of the derived update in the tested cases, while the control extensions are explicitly presented as preliminary investigations.
neurips-2007-temporal-difference-updatin.tldr: A statistically derived temporal-difference rule replaces a free learning-rate parameter with a transition-specific equation and improves reported experimental performance.

paragraphs: Testing homogeneity asks whether two samples could come from the same underlying distribution. This paper approaches that question using kernel Fisher discriminant analysis. A method associated with separating groups becomes the basis of a statistical test, connecting evidence of distinguishability with the question of whether the samples are homogeneous.

The authors construct a consistent nonparametric test statistic. Nonparametric testing avoids specifying a fixed parametric family for the distributions being compared. Consistency concerns the test’s behavior as the amount of data grows, so it is a long-run statistical property rather than a promise of correct decisions for every pair of finite samples.

The paper also derives the statistic’s asymptotic distribution under the null hypothesis of homogeneity. That describes its limiting behavior when the samples share a distribution, providing a theoretical reference for interpreting the statistic. Experiments on artificial and real datasets give evidence of the method’s relevance. Together, the construction, consistency result, and null-distribution analysis turn a discriminant-analysis approach into a theoretically supported two-sample test.
neurips-2007-testing-for-homogeneity-wit.tldr: Kernel Fisher discriminant analysis yields a consistent nonparametric homogeneity test with a derived asymptotic null distribution.

paragraphs: A multi-armed bandit learner repeatedly chooses actions while learning from their rewards. Observable side information adds context that can help guide those choices. This paper introduces Epoch-Greedy for that setting and relates its performance to the difficulty of supervised learning over a chosen hypothesis class.

The algorithm does not require advance knowledge of the time horizon T, meaning the number of rounds need not be specified beforehand. Its regret is controlled by a sample-complexity bound for the hypothesis class. Regret measures accumulated loss relative to a comparison strategy, while sample complexity describes how much data supervised learning needs.

The stated regret scaling is O(T^(2/3) S^(1/3)) or better, where S is the complexity term in a standard supervised-learning sample-complexity bound. Some cases can be much better. The result connects sequential decision-making performance to a familiar learning-theoretic quantity: the complexity of learning within the selected class. It also provides a guarantee for an algorithm that can operate without a preselected stopping horizon.
neurips-2007-the-epoch-greedy-algorithm-.tldr: Epoch-Greedy needs no known time horizon and links contextual-bandit regret to supervised-learning sample complexity.

paragraphs: Online handwriting recognition records the movement of the pen directly. Even with that information, recognizing letters is difficult because a single letter extends across many recorded pen positions. Conventional sequence-labeling approaches such as hidden Markov models therefore require sophisticated preprocessing to turn the raw trajectory into suitable inputs.

This paper presents a system that can transcribe the raw handwriting sequence directly. It combines a recurrent neural network trained for sequence labeling with a probabilistic language model. The network handles the recorded sequence, while the language model contributes information about plausible text sequences to the overall recognition system.

Experiments on an unconstrained online handwriting database report strong results with both raw and preprocessed input. In each case, the system substantially outperforms the benchmark hidden Markov model. The raw-input result is particularly relevant to the paper’s motivation: the proposed combination can operate directly on pen data despite each character spanning multiple observations. The preprocessed-input result shows that its reported advantage also holds when preprocessing is supplied.
neurips-2007-unconstrained-on-line-handw.tldr: A recurrent network combined with a language model directly transcribes pen trajectories and outperforms a benchmark HMM on raw and preprocessed handwriting.

paragraphs: A Gaussian process uses a covariance kernel to express relationships between inputs. This paper learns that kernel using features from a deep belief network trained on unlabeled data. The approach connects representation learning with Gaussian-process prediction, making the learned description of the input part of the covariance model.

The first stage learns a deep generative model through a fast greedy training procedure. A Gaussian kernel is then applied to features in the network’s top layer. For high-dimensional, highly structured data, the authors report that this works much better than applying a similar kernel directly to raw inputs. The advantage is stated for that kind of data.

A further stage uses backpropagation through the deep belief network to fine-tune the covariance kernel discriminatively. The authors report additional improvements for both regression and classification. The overall method thus uses unlabeled data to learn structure and then adjusts the representation for prediction. Its key finding is that the feature space in which a kernel operates can substantially affect Gaussian-process performance.
neurips-2007-using-deep-belief-nets-to-l.tldr: Deep belief network features improve Gaussian-process kernels for highly structured, high-dimensional data, with further gains from discriminative fine-tuning.
